'''Daniel McGillivray Brown''' FRS (3 February 1923 – 24 April 2012) was a Scottish [[nucleic acid]] [[chemist]].

==Early life and career==

Daniel McGillivray Brown was born in [[Giffnock]] on 3 February 1923, son of David Cunninghame Brown, a restaurateur,  and Catherine Stewart (née McGillivray), a teacher. After Giffnock Primary School he attended [[The Glasgow Academy|Glasgow Academy]] and then, at age 17, [[Glasgow University]] where he studied chemistry, and received an honours degree.<ref name=frs>{{cite journal | title=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society: Daniel McGillivray Brown. 3 February 1923—24 April 2012 | author=Michael J. Gait | date=7 November 2018 | doi=10.1098/rsbm.2018.0008 | s2cid=81639128 | doi-access=free }}</ref>

In 1945 Brown moved to the [[Institute of Cancer Research#1909 to 1970|Chester Beatty Research Institute]], then in [[Chelsea, London|Chelsea]], where he worked on the synthesis of heterocyclic stilbene derivatives for his PhD.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Brown|first1=Daniel M|last2=Kon|first2=George A R|title=Some heterocyclic analogues of stilbenes|journal=Journal of the Chemical Society|pages=2147–2154|date=1948|doi=10.1039/jr9480002147}}</ref>
Then, in 1948, Brown moved to Cambridge to join [[Alexander R. Todd|Alexander Todd]]’s group. He gained his second PhD in 1952.<ref name=Kings>{{Cite journal|title=Obituaries: Daniel McGillivray Brown (1953)|journal=King's College, Cambridge Annual Report 2013|pages=72–75}}</ref> Brown was appointed lecturer in the chemistry department in 1959, and reader in 1967. He was Visiting Professor at [[University of California, Los Angeles]] 1959–60;  and at [[Brandeis University]] 1966–67.<ref>{{Who's Who |id=9780199540884.013.U8977 |title=Brown, Dr Daniel McGillivray}}</ref> He received the Sc.D in 1968, and eventually became Vice-Provost at Kings College in 1974.

In 1981 Brown took a sabbatical at the [[MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology|Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB)]], and then moved there permanently one year later. He retired formally from the LMB in 2002 but continued publishing until 2008.<ref name=Kings/>

==Contributions==

At Cambridge, Brown set out to confirm the furanose chemical structure of the sugar part of nucleosides in natural nucleic acids, which had only been inferred at the time. He and Basil Lythgoe proved this to be the case.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Brown|first1=D M|last2=Lythgoe|first2=B R|title=Deoxyribonucleosides and related compounds. Part II. A proof of the furanose structure of the natural 2-deoxyribonucleosides|journal=Journal of the Chemical Society|pages=1990–1991|date=1950|doi=10.1039/jr9500001990}}</ref> He later worked on the selective phosphorylation of nucleosides to form nucleotides. This was the beginning of a lifelong career, and led to the chemical structures of RNA and, by inference, DNA. He later worked on [[Phosphatidylinositol#Phosphoinositides|phosphoinositides]] and the [[mutagenesis]] of nucleotides. 

==Personal life==

Daniel Brown met Margaret Joyce Herbert at Scottish Highland Dancing classes at the CUSRC<ref>{{cite web|title=The Cambridge University Strathspey and Reel Club|website= Cambridge University Strathspey and Reel Club |url= https://cusarc.soc.srcf.net|access-date=18 August 2020}}</ref> in 1952. They married in Lincolnshire the following year. Dan and Margaret had four children: Catherine (1954), David (1955), Frances (1961) and Moira (1962). 

Daniel McGillivray Brown died at his home in Cambridge on 24 April 2012.<ref name=Kings/> He was survived by his wife, three daughters, four grandchildren and a great grand-daughter.<ref>{{Cite web|title= Dr Daniel Brown |website=The Herald|url=https://www.heraldscotland.com/opinion/13057977.dr-daniel-brown|date=15 May 2012|access-date=20 August 2020}}</ref>

==Honors==

Brown became a Fellow of the [[Royal Society]] in 1982.
